title: Dow Hill, Kurseong: Schools, Forest and Ghost Stories
meta_description: Dow Hill above Kurseong: the 1879 Victoria School, the conifer forest, the headless boy and other ghost stories told as lore, and the walk to Chimney.
summary: Dow Hill is the forested ridge above Kurseong, home to Victoria Boys' School, founded in 1879, and Dow Hill School. Its quiet conifer forest has made it famous for ghost stories, from a headless boy to footsteps in empty corridors, which we tell as local lore. Walk up from Kurseong in 1–1.5 hours, then on to Chimney.

sections.heading: The hill above Kurseong
paras: Dow Hill rises behind Kurseong bazaar to about 1,900 m, some 400 m above the station. A road climbs from town past the post office and through a forest of tall conifers and broadleaf trees to a ridge where two old boarding schools stand a short distance apart. Beyond them the road continues through more forest to Chimney and Bagora, following roughly the line of the old road to Darjeeling that predates the Hill Cart Road.

For most of the year it is simply a beautiful walk: quiet, cool and often wrapped in mist by early afternoon. But Dow Hill has another reputation. Newspapers, television programmes and travel lists have called it one of the most haunted places in India, and every driver in Kurseong has a story to tell. This guide gives you both: the real history of the hill and the folklore, clearly marked as folklore.

sections.heading: The schools and the forest
paras: In 1879 Sir Ashley Eden, then Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, wanted a hill school for the children of government servants of modest income, the clerks and railway staff of the province, who could not afford the expensive schools of Darjeeling. The result was Victoria School on Dow Hill, now Victoria Boys' School, built in stone in the cool forest above Kurseong. A girls' school followed on the same ridge in the late nineteenth century and grew into Dow Hill School. Both are still working boarding schools, and their chapels and long stone buildings set the tone of the hill.

The forest around them is managed by the forest department, and Dow Hill has long had a forestry presence, including forest offices and a small forest museum on the ridge. The museum, when open, displays timber samples, preserved animals and exhibits on the hill forests; opening hours have varied, so check current status before you travel. The schools do not admit visitors without permission, but the public road passes their gates, and in term time you will hear assemblies and games from the road.

sections.heading: The ghost stories, told as lore
paras: What follows is the local story, told by drivers, shopkeepers and former pupils, not anything found in a record. The best known is the headless boy: a young figure said to be seen walking along the forest road and then vanishing into the trees. Some woodcutters and walkers, the story goes, have followed him a few steps before he disappeared. A second tale is of a woman in grey seen on the road near the girls' school, and a third of footsteps and voices in the corridors of Victoria Boys' School during the long winter holidays, when the buildings stand empty from December to February.

The stretch of road between Dow Hill Road and the forest office is called the 'death road' by some local people, and stories attach to it of travellers feeling watched or followed. You will hear different versions from each teller, and details change as the stories pass from one person to the next. We have found no historical event behind any of them. What is real is the setting: dense, dark conifer forest, a winding road with few houses, thick afternoon mist and, in winter, schools that fall completely silent. Those are reason enough for stories to grow.

sections.heading: Walking Dow Hill and on to Chimney
paras: The classic walk starts in Kurseong bazaar. Walk up past the post office towards Dow Hill Road; it is about 3–5 km and 1–1.5 hours uphill to the schools, on a road with light traffic. From the schools, the forest road continues to Chimney, roughly 2,200 m, where a lone brick chimney of about 7 m is all that is left of a dak bungalow that local accounts date to about 1839. The full walk from Kurseong to Chimney takes about 3–3.5 hours and climbs roughly 700 m.

Many walkers go up on foot and come down by taxi or local jeep. A Kurseong taxi costs about ₹400–600 one way to Dow Hill, or ₹1,200–1,800 for a half-day loop to Dow Hill, Chimney and back. A few local jeeps run between Kurseong and Bagora via Dow Hill and Chimney, mainly in the morning and late afternoon, for small fares; ask at the Kurseong stand the day before. For a quieter night in the same forest, stay in one of Chimney's family homestays at about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals.

sections.heading: When to go and what to expect
paras: October to December gives clear mornings and dry paths, and on good days the snow peaks show through gaps in the forest. March and April bring new leaf and birdsong. The mist that gives Dow Hill its mood comes most afternoons from April to September, and in the monsoon the road can be wet, the forest full of leeches and visibility down to a few metres. In December and January the ridge is 3–5 °C colder than Kurseong, close to freezing at Chimney at night.

The best time of day for the walk is morning, starting by 8 or 9 am, so you are back in town or at Chimney before the mist and the dark. Carry water, a light jacket and a torch. There are only one or two tea stalls along the way, selling tea and biscuits for ₹30–60. Phone signal is patchy in the deepest stretches of forest, so tell someone in your hotel which way you are going.

sections.heading: Visiting with respect
paras: Dow Hill is a place where children live and study, and the stories should not get in the way of that. A few simple rules make a visit easy for everyone.
list: Do not enter the school campuses or photograph pupils without permission
Do not wander the forest at night looking for ghosts; roads are unlit and the forest is home to wild animals
Keep to the road and marked paths; side trails are steep and easy to lose in mist
Keep noise low near the schools during term time
Take your rubbish back to town
Treat the stories as stories, and ask locals for theirs over tea rather than pushing for drama

sections.heading: Combining Dow Hill with the rest of Kurseong
paras: Dow Hill fits into a full day in Kurseong. Start early with the walk up, continue to Chimney if you have the legs, and come back by taxi for lunch in the bazaar. In the afternoon, take a car or a long walk to the Netaji museum at Giddapahar, a few kilometres below town, or go down the Pankhabari road to Makaibari tea estate. Finish at Eagle's Crag above the station for the evening view down the Hill Cart Road.

If you have two days, split them: Dow Hill and Chimney with a night in a Chimney homestay, then a morning walk down through the forest and an afternoon at Makaibari. It is one of the best short walking trips in the Darjeeling hills, and it costs very little beyond your bed and meals.

faqs.a: Dow Hill is famous for ghost stories, but they are folklore rather than recorded history. The best known are a headless boy who vanishes into the forest, a woman in grey and footsteps in empty school corridors in the winter holidays. We have found no historical event behind them. The dense forest and afternoon mist explain why the stories grew.

faqs.q: What is the headless boy story of Dow Hill?
faqs.a: The local story says a headless boy is sometimes seen walking along the forest road on Dow Hill before disappearing among the trees, and that some walkers and woodcutters have followed him a few steps. It is told by drivers, shopkeepers and former pupils, with details that change from teller to teller. It is lore, not a documented event.

faqs.q: How do I get to Dow Hill from Kurseong?
faqs.a: Walk up from Kurseong bazaar past the post office along Dow Hill Road, about 3–5 km and 1–1.5 hours uphill, on a road with light traffic. A taxi costs about ₹400–600 one way, or ₹1,200–1,800 for a half-day loop to Dow Hill, Chimney and back. A few local jeeps also run towards Bagora via Dow Hill.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit Victoria Boys' School and Dow Hill School?
faqs.a: Not without permission. Both are working boarding schools, and their campuses are closed to casual visitors. The public road passes their gates, so you can see the old stone buildings and chapels from outside. Please do not photograph pupils or walk into the grounds. Former pupils and parents visit by arrangement with the schools.

faqs.q: When was Victoria Boys' School founded?
faqs.a: Victoria Boys' School, originally Victoria School, was founded on Dow Hill in 1879 at the wish of Sir Ashley Eden, Lieutenant-Governor of Bengal, for the children of government servants of modest income. A girls' school followed on the same ridge in the late nineteenth century and became Dow Hill School. Both are still running.

faqs.q: Is the Dow Hill forest museum open?
faqs.a: Dow Hill has a small forest museum run under the forest department, with timber samples, preserved animals and exhibits on the hill forests. Opening hours and days have varied over the years, and it has sometimes been closed. Ask in Kurseong or at the forest office before you go, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk on Dow Hill?
faqs.a: Yes, in daylight. The road from Kurseong is quiet and used by locals, schoolchildren and walkers. Start in the morning, carry water and a jacket, and return before dark, when the road is unlit. In the monsoon the road is slippery and leeches are common. Avoid side trails in mist, as they are steep and easy to lose.

faqs.q: How far is Chimney from Dow Hill?
faqs.a: Chimney lies along the same forest road beyond the Dow Hill schools, at about 2,200 m. From the schools it is roughly 1.5–2 hours more on foot; the whole walk from Kurseong bazaar to Chimney takes about 3–3.5 hours and climbs about 700 m. A taxi from Kurseong to Chimney costs about ₹700–1,000 and takes 20–30 minutes.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Dow Hill?
faqs.a: October to December gives clear mornings and dry paths, and March to April brings new leaf and birds. Go in the morning, before the afternoon mist settles. In the monsoon the forest is wet, leech-filled and often fogged in. Winter is cold on the ridge, so carry warm layers from December to February.
